Summary: Foundation: private repository and upstream tracking
Description: Stand up the private repository extracted from matchamfraser/legalworkflows at commit 8b3466f, with the remote topology that keeps upstream security fixes mergeable. The fork is currently at exact parity with upstream - 581 commits, no divergence - so this is the cheapest moment to get the structure right.
Acceptance Criteria: Private repo exists and is protected; a clean clone builds; upstream-main mirrors upstream and merges fast-forward.

Summary: Extract into a private repository with history intact
Description: Clone the full tree with history rather than copying files. History is what makes upstream merges possible and is the cleanest record of what changed and when, which AGPL section 5(a) asks you to state. Do NOT squash or re-init.
Acceptance Criteria: git log on backend/src/app.ts shows pre-extraction commits; npm ci and npm run build pass from a clean clone.

Summary: Clone with full history and rewire remotes
Description: git clone the existing fork, then: rename origin to fork, add upstream = Open-Legal-Products/legalworkflows, add origin = the new private repo. Three remotes, each with one job. Push main to the new origin.
Acceptance Criteria: git remote -v shows all three; git log --oneline | wc -l returns 581.

Summary: Create the protected upstream-main mirror branch
Description: Branch upstream-main from upstream/main and push it. Nothing is ever committed to this branch - it exists only as a clean merge base. Protect it to allow fast-forward pushes only, so it cannot drift.
Acceptance Criteria: upstream-main exists on origin; a non-fast-forward push to it is rejected.

Summary: Configure branch protection and merge rules on main
Description: Protect main: require a PR, require status checks to pass, require branches up to date before merging, no force push, auto-delete merged branches. Solo development still benefits - this is what makes CI actually gate anything.
Acceptance Criteria: Direct push to main is rejected; a PR with red CI cannot merge.

Summary: Add fork-specific rules to AGENTS.md
Description: The repo already carries a strong AGENTS.md. Add a section at the top covering the four constraints specific to this fork: the HTTP-only service boundary to Juralio, the user-visible-only rename rule with its do-not-touch list, the additive-changes-in-new-files merge rule, and the rule that LICENSE is never deleted or altered.
Acceptance Criteria: AGENTS.md states all four rules; both the developer and Claude Code are bound by them from the first commit.

Summary: Establish and prove the upstream merge routine
Description: Upstream merged 581 commits in roughly four months. A sync routine that is documented and exercised once now is far cheaper than one improvised in six months against a large diff.
Acceptance Criteria: A documented three-command sync exists and has been run end to end at least once.

Summary: Document and script the upstream sync
Description: fetch upstream, fast-forward upstream-main, merge upstream-main into main, resolve, test, push. Note the .gitattributes convention already in the repo: package-lock.json is merged as binary deliberately, so conflicts surface explicitly - resolve by taking main's copy and regenerating.
Acceptance Criteria: docs/upstream-sync.md exists; the routine is reproducible from it alone.

Summary: Run a first upstream merge as a dry run
Description: Execute the routine before any local divergence exists, so the mechanics are proven while a conflict is impossible. Records a baseline merge commit.
Acceptance Criteria: Merge completes; full backend and frontend suites green afterwards.

Summary: Unblock the build
Description: Two inherited dependencies stop the project dead on a restricted network. Neither is a code defect, both must be cleared before any CI work can be validated. Verified in review: npm ci fails with a 403 today.
Acceptance Criteria: npm ci completes on a filtered network; all 117 backend test files run, not 80.

Summary: Remove the SheetJS CDN dependency
Description: backend/package.json pins xlsx to https://cdn.sheetjs.com/xlsx-0.20.3/xlsx-0.20.3.tgz - a direct vendor tarball, not a registry package. Any proxy or air-gapped runner fails npm ci outright, and Dependabot cannot see it. Only backend/src/lib/spreadsheet.ts imports it.
Acceptance Criteria: npm ci --prefix backend succeeds behind an egress filter; spreadsheet parsing behaviour is unchanged.

Summary: Replace xlsx with exceljs in spreadsheet.ts
Description: exceljs is already a frontend dependency, so it is a known quantity. Preserve the current output contract exactly: a cell-addressed markdown table per sheet, using the Excel-formatted display string (cell.w equivalent) so dates and currency reach the model as a human sees them, with cached formula results rather than formulas.
Acceptance Criteria: Existing spreadsheet tests pass unchanged; a sample .xlsx, .xlsm and legacy .xls each produce identical output to the previous implementation.

Summary: Verify a clean install and the full backend suite
Description: Confirm the fix on a network that blocks non-registry hosts. Before this ticket, 31 of 117 backend test files cannot be exercised at all.
Acceptance Criteria: npm ci, npm run build and npm test all pass; test file count is 117, not 80.

Summary: Take ownership of the workflow catalogue
Description: System assistant and tabular-review workflows are not in this tree. A sync job downloads them at runtime from Open-Legal-Products/mike-workflows, and five defaults are hardcoded by key in backend/src/lib/workflowCatalogSource.ts. Product content is therefore controlled by a third party.
Acceptance Criteria: The catalogue syncs from a repository you control; upstream renaming or privatising theirs has no effect.

Summary: Fork mike-workflows and repoint the sync
Description: Fork the catalogue repository and set MIKE_WORKFLOWS_REPOSITORY to the fork. Check the catalogue repo's own licence first - it is a separate repository and may not be AGPL. The ingestion code is already hardened with size caps, path validation and timeouts, so this is configuration, not a rewrite.
Acceptance Criteria: Sync job pulls from the fork; workflows appear in the app; the catalogue repo licence is recorded.

Summary: Verify catalogue sync end to end
Description: Run the sync job against an empty database and confirm the five defaults install, quick actions resolve, and add-ons appear in the catalogue.
Acceptance Criteria: Fresh database reaches a populated workflow catalogue with no manual steps.

Summary: CI/CD adaptation
Description: Nine of the eleven inherited workflows carry over, one must be deleted because it cannot work on a private repo, and one is optional. The inherited suite is unusually strong - mutation testing, a real-Supabase security suite and a schema drift check - and is worth preserving intact.
Acceptance Criteria: CI green on every PR; the security suites are required checks; no workflow fails for reasons unrelated to the code.

Summary: Port the inherited workflows to the private repo
Description: Adapt the eleven workflows to the new repo topology and plan constraints.
Acceptance Criteria: Every retained workflow runs green; deleted and disabled ones are documented with the reason.

Summary: Delete scorecard.yml and retarget branch filters
Description: scorecard.yml sets publish_results: true against the OpenSSF public API, which only accepts public repositories - it cannot work here. Separately, e2e.yml already filters on [main, upstream-main], which matches the topology from the foundation epic; confirm rather than change.
Acceptance Criteria: scorecard.yml removed with the reason in the commit message; e2e branch filter verified correct.

Summary: Configure Actions secrets and verify the e2e run
Description: Create ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (spend-capped, CI-scoped) for e2e.yml and LOADTEST_AUTH_TOKEN if the k6 job is retained. The e2e workflow boots Supabase, RustFS and Playwright on the runner, so this is the longest feedback loop to prove.
Acceptance Criteria: e2e workflow completes green on a pull request.

Summary: Enable Dependabot and confirm the advisory gate
Description: .github/dependabot.yml already ships. On a private repo, Dependabot alerts and security updates must be enabled explicitly under Settings > Advanced Security. It pairs with security.yml, which fails the build on a high or critical advisory.
Acceptance Criteria: Dependabot opens a PR against a seeded outdated dependency; security.yml fails the build on a known advisory.

Summary: Confirm CodeQL availability on the account plan
Description: CodeQL on private repositories requires GitHub Advanced Security on some plans. Establish whether it runs; if not, record the gap and decide whether to buy the capability or accept the loss.
Acceptance Criteria: codeql.yml either runs green or is disabled with a documented decision.

Summary: Disable the Word add-in workflow while the add-in is deferred
Description: word-addin.yml runs Playwright against chromium and webkit. The add-in stays in the repo but is out of scope for these 24 weeks, so the job is noise. Disable rather than delete - it is re-enabled when the add-in is picked up.
Acceptance Criteria: Workflow disabled with a comment naming the sprint it should return in.

Summary: Make the security suites required checks
Description: These are the gates that catch real damage on a service-role architecture. Protecting the branch without them is theatre.
Acceptance Criteria: A PR cannot merge with any of them red.

Summary: Require stack-tests, schema-drift, gitleaks and CI
Description: stack-tests boots a real Supabase and asserts the deny-all RLS firewall holds for anon and authenticated clients - the only backstop for an architecture where the backend runs as service role. schema-drift compares a fresh database against an upgraded one. gitleaks scans full history.
Acceptance Criteria: All four are required status checks on main; each has run green at least once.

Summary: Keep mutation testing running against the security libs
Description: Stryker is scoped to access.ts, downloadTokens.ts and chat/citations.ts - the places where a hollow test is dangerous. It runs monthly as a drift check and does not gate merges upstream; keep that posture.
Acceptance Criteria: Mutation workflow runs and its report is retrievable; the scoped file list is unchanged.

Summary: Debranding
Description: Strip the upstream trademark from user-visible surfaces while leaving internal identifiers alone. About 260 files mention the name; only a few dozen are user-visible. Renaming database objects, environment variables or the API client buys nothing and guarantees conflicts on every upstream merge.
Acceptance Criteria: No upstream trademark appears in any user-visible surface; database, env var and module names are unchanged; all suites green.

Summary: Replace user-visible branding in the web app
Description: Work file by file from the identified list. Do NOT run a repo-wide find-and-replace: it will hit comments, test fixtures, table names and the API client, and unpicking it costs more than doing it properly.
Acceptance Criteria: Wordmark, metadata, MFA issuer and user-facing copy all carry the new brand; frontend build and 980 tests green.

Summary: Replace the wordmark and application metadata
Description: frontend/src/app/components/site-logo.tsx carries the wordmark. frontend/src/app/layout.tsx carries the Open Graph siteName and image alt text. Both are rendered to users and to link previews.
Acceptance Criteria: Wordmark and OG metadata show the new brand; a shared link preview renders correctly.

Summary: Change the MFA issuer name
Description: settings/security/page.tsx passes the brand to enrollMfa, which becomes the account label inside users' authenticator apps. Changing it after users enrol is disruptive, so it must be right before the first real account exists.
Acceptance Criteria: A newly enrolled TOTP factor shows the new brand in the authenticator app.

Summary: Update user-facing copy across settings and modals
Description: settings/personalisation, tabular/AddColumnModal, workflows/WFEditColumnModal, shared/AddUserInput and assistant error text all name the assistant in copy shown to users.
Acceptance Criteria: No user-visible string names the upstream product; copy reads naturally with the new name.

Summary: Replace icon components and image assets
Description: MikeIconUI.tsx in shared/ui, chat/mike-icon.tsx, and the marketing images under docs/assets. Keep the component filenames if you are tracking upstream - only the rendered artwork needs to change.
Acceptance Criteria: New mark renders in the app and add-in; upstream screenshots deleted from docs/assets.

Summary: Update Word add-in surfaces
Description: word-addin WordAddinLogo.tsx is the branded lockup; EditCard.tsx and useWordDoc.ts carry user-facing strings naming the assistant. In scope even though the add-in is not shipped, so the brand is consistent when it is picked up.
Acceptance Criteria: Add-in task pane shows the new brand; typecheck passes.

Summary: Fix the rename boundary in writing
Description: Without a written rule, the next rename will reach into the database and the merge cost becomes permanent.
Acceptance Criteria: The do-not-rename list is in AGENTS.md and has survived one upstream merge.

Summary: Record the do-not-rename identifiers
Description: Four categories stay as they are: the mike_workflows and mike_workflow_assets tables with their 11 indexes and constraints; the MIKE_WORKFLOWS_REPOSITORY, _REF and _TOKEN environment variables; mikeApi.ts, which is 2,837 lines imported across the frontend; and the private package names. Each is invisible to users and expensive to change.
Acceptance Criteria: AGENTS.md lists all four with the reasoning; a reviewer can apply the rule without asking.

Summary: Verify the rebrand against a full build and suite
Description: A find-and-replace error in this area typically surfaces as a broken import or a failed snapshot rather than a visible bug.
Acceptance Criteria: frontend build, 141 test files, backend suite and lint all green; manual pass over every rebranded screen.

Summary: Infrastructure foundation
Description: Provision the managed services the platform needs, as code where possible, with staging and production separated from the start. This is client-confidential legal material, so the two environments never share a database, a bucket or a secret.
Acceptance Criteria: Staging and production both provisioned; schema loaded and drift-checked; secrets generated per environment.

Summary: Provision Supabase and load the schema
Description: backend/schema.sql is the complete fresh-install schema at 4,906 lines covering 50 tables; backend/migrations/ holds 85 dated incremental files. A fresh install loads the schema; an existing deployment applies only migrations newer than its recorded version, in filename order.
Acceptance Criteria: Both environments reach an identical schema; the drift check passes fresh against upgraded.

Summary: Create staging and production Supabase projects
Description: Separate projects, separate credentials, separate regions if data residency requires it. Never point staging at production data.
Acceptance Criteria: Two projects exist with no shared credentials; access is documented.

Summary: Load the schema and verify RLS is deny-all
Description: RLS is enabled on 30 tables and defined with zero policies - deliberately deny-all, so a leaked publishable key reaches nothing. Confirm this holds on the real projects, not just in CI.
Acceptance Criteria: An anon client and a signed-in user client both return zero rows from every table; the service role reads normally.

Summary: Configure auth: providers, email delivery and MFA
Description: Auth flows need working email before anyone can be onboarded. Configure the mailer, the redirect URLs, Google OAuth if wanted, and confirm the MFA enrolment path end to end.
Acceptance Criteria: Signup, password reset and MFA enrolment all complete against staging.

Summary: Provision object storage
Description: S3-compatible storage holds every uploaded document. Direct browser uploads use presigned URLs, so CORS must be right or uploads fail in a way that looks like an application bug.
Acceptance Criteria: Documents upload, convert, download and delete correctly in staging.

Summary: Create buckets and apply the CORS policy
Description: docker/storage-cors.json is the template shipped for the local stack; apply its equivalent to the real bucket. Separate buckets per environment.
Acceptance Criteria: A direct browser upload to staging succeeds from the application origin and is refused from another origin.

Summary: Verify the signed-URL round trip
Description: Upload signing, download tokens and the tamper-evident export manifest all depend on correct storage configuration. Download tokens are HMAC-SHA256 with timing-safe comparison; each signed URL authorises only its own object key.
Acceptance Criteria: Upload, signed download and manifest verification all succeed; a tampered token is rejected.

Summary: Secrets and configuration management
Description: Four secrets must be generated per environment and never reused between them or derived from the Supabase key.
Acceptance Criteria: Every environment has distinct high-entropy secrets held in a secret store, not in a repo or a shell history.

Summary: Generate per-environment secrets
Description: openssl rand -hex 32 for each of DOWNLOAD_SIGNING_SECRET (HMAC for /download/:token), USER_API_KEYS_ENCRYPTION_SECRET (AES-256-GCM for stored per-user provider keys), AUTH_HANDOFF_ENCRYPTION_SECRET (only if the Word add-in is deployed) and MANIFEST_SIGNING_KEY (export signing).
Acceptance Criteria: Four distinct secrets per environment, stored in the platform secret manager; none appears in the repo.

Summary: Wire configuration into the deploy target
Description: Backend reads roughly 50 environment variables. The frontend needs only three: API_BASE_URL, NODE_ENV and one feature flag. Keep every backend secret out of NEXT_PUBLIC_* - that prefix ships to the browser.
Acceptance Criteria: Both services start from injected configuration with no local .env; a grep proves no secret is under a NEXT_PUBLIC_ name.

Summary: Deployment pipeline
Description: Get the service running in staging with a safe, repeatable deploy path. The backend is a standalone Express service with its own Dockerfile and entrypoint, so this is conventional container work with one wrinkle: it needs LibreOffice on the path.
Acceptance Criteria: A tagged commit reaches staging automatically; rollback is tested; migrations never race.

Summary: Containerise and deploy the backend
Description: backend/Dockerfile exists. backend/railpack.json declares the extra system packages needed - libreoffice and fonts-liberation - which must be replicated on whatever host is chosen, or DOC/DOCX to PDF conversion fails at runtime rather than at build time.
Acceptance Criteria: Image builds, scans clean and runs in staging with document conversion working.

Summary: Build and scan the backend image
Description: Include LibreOffice and fonts-liberation. Add an image vulnerability scan to the pipeline and fail on high or critical findings, consistent with the existing npm advisory gate.
Acceptance Criteria: Image builds in CI, scan is green, a DOCX converts to PDF inside the running container.

Summary: Deploy to staging with migrate-then-start ordering
Description: Migrations must complete before the new backend version starts, and must not run concurrently from multiple instances. Deploy order is migrate, then backend, then frontend if it is deployed at all.
Acceptance Criteria: A deploy from a clean state applies migrations exactly once and starts healthy.

Summary: Add health checks, rollback and deploy gating
Description: The service exposes GET /health. Wire it to the platform health check, prove a rollback to the previous image, and gate the deploy on CI being green for that commit.
Acceptance Criteria: A deliberately broken deploy is caught by the health check and rolled back without manual intervention.

Summary: Decide the disposition of the inherited frontend
Description: Mike's Next.js app is not the customer-facing product - Juralio is. But mikeApi.ts is a 2,837-line typed client that documents the API contract, and the Playwright e2e suite drives the real flows through it. Keeping it in the repo is free; deploying it is a decision.
Acceptance Criteria: A decision is recorded, and the e2e suite still runs whichever way it goes.

Summary: Deploy as an internal admin surface, or retire it
Description: Recommended: deploy behind authentication as an internal operations and support console. It gives you a working UI for every backend capability at no build cost. If retired instead, the e2e suite needs a CI-only build target so it keeps running.
Acceptance Criteria: Either an internal surface is live and access-controlled, or e2e runs against a CI-only build with the decision documented.

Summary: Security remediation
Description: The findings from the repository assessment that must be closed before any environment holds real client documents. The codebase starts strong - AES-256-GCM key storage, timing-safe token comparison, a thorough SSRF blocklist, helmet, twelve rate limiters - so this is closing specific gaps, not a rebuild.
Acceptance Criteria: Audit trail answers who could see what and since when; no route reaches data without an access check; production limits configured.

Summary: Close the audit trail gaps
Description: Eighteen actions are audited today, covering chat turns, document edits, uploads, exports, organisation membership and invitations. Nothing records who granted or revoked access to a project, and nothing records authentication events. For software holding privileged material, those are the two questions you will actually be asked.
Acceptance Criteria: Share grants, revocations and authentication events all appear in the audit trail and in the export.

Summary: Audit project share grant and revoke
Description: recordAudit in backend/src/lib/audit.ts is the insertion point. Add calls in lib/projectAccess.ts covering upsertProjectGrant, deleteProjectGrant and removeGrantsForEmail, recording actor, subject, resource and the resulting role.
Acceptance Criteria: Granting and revoking access each write an audit event naming actor, subject and role; both appear in the audit export.

Summary: Audit authentication events
Description: Login, logout, failed login, password reset, MFA enrolment and MFA removal. These are the events a client security questionnaire asks about by name.
Acceptance Criteria: Each event type is recorded with timestamp, actor and source; failures are distinguishable from successes.

Summary: Harden the service-role authorisation boundary
Description: Because the backend runs as service role against a policy-free schema, correctness rests entirely on developers remembering to call the access helpers. A new endpoint that forgets ensureDocAccess is a cross-tenant data leak, not a permission error. There is no database backstop underneath.
Acceptance Criteria: Every route with a tenant-scoped resource has a test proving another tenant is denied.

Summary: Add cross-tenant denial tests for every route
Description: Work the route list systematically. The pattern exists already in the integration suite; extend it so each endpoint has a case where user B requests user A's resource and receives a denial, not data.
Acceptance Criteria: Every tenant-scoped endpoint has a cross-tenant denial test; deliberately removing an access check turns a test red.

Summary: Add a review checklist for unguarded service-role queries
Description: A lint rule or documented PR checklist that flags a createServerSupabase query with no accompanying access-helper call in the same handler. Cheap insurance against the failure mode the architecture invites.
Acceptance Criteria: The check exists and has been exercised against a deliberately unguarded query.

Summary: Production security baseline
Description: Configuration that is correct for local development and wrong for the internet.
Acceptance Criteria: Origins, limits and data policies are set for production and documented.

Summary: Configure origins and rate limits for production
Description: backend/src/app.ts already carries helmet, a CORS allowlist and twelve distinct rate limiters, all tunable by environment variable. Set them for real traffic rather than accepting the development defaults, and confirm NODE_ENV=production only with HTTPS public URLs.
Acceptance Criteria: CORS rejects an unknown origin; each limiter is set deliberately with the value recorded.

Summary: Document storage retention, logging and deletion behaviour
Description: What is stored, where, for how long, what is logged, and what actually happens on deletion. userDataCleanup.ts is 1,008 lines and defines the real deletion behaviour - document it rather than describing an intention.
Acceptance Criteria: A written policy exists that matches the code; it is good enough to answer a client security questionnaire.

Summary: Integration with the Juralio platform
Description: Wire the Apache-2.0 matter management platform to this service. The seam already exists and is clean: backend/ and frontend/ share no code, no npm workspace links them, and the only channel is HTTP via API_BASE_URL. Juralio becomes a second consumer of the same contract.
Acceptance Criteria: Juralio calls the workflow service over HTTP for a real end-to-end flow; no code crosses the boundary in either direction.

Summary: Build the HTTP client seam in Juralio
Description: Mike's own BFF proxy - frontend/src/app/api/[...path]/route.ts, 78 lines - is the reference pattern: it forwards the HttpOnly cookie session upstream so no key ever reaches the browser. Write Juralio's equivalent rather than importing that one.
Acceptance Criteria: Juralio reaches the workflow service through its own proxy; no credential is exposed to the browser.

Summary: Write Juralio's proxy to the workflow service
Description: Forward the session, set forwarded-host and forwarded-proto, stream request and response bodies, no-store caching, manual redirect handling. Target the service base URL from configuration, never hardcoded.
Acceptance Criteria: A request from Juralio reaches the service and streams the response back, including SSE.

Summary: Re-declare the API types on the Juralio side
Description: Do NOT import Mike's types. Write the interfaces Juralio needs against the eighteen route prefixes it actually consumes. A few hundred lines of interface, and it is what keeps the two works legally separate.
Acceptance Criteria: Juralio typechecks with no dependency on the service repo; the types match the live API.

Summary: Map identity and sessions between the two systems
Description: Decide how a Juralio user becomes a workflow-service principal: shared identity provider, token exchange, or per-request assertion. This choice determines whether the audit trail can attribute actions to a real person.
Acceptance Criteria: A Juralio user's actions appear in the service audit trail attributed to them, not to a service account.

Summary: Enforce the boundary in CI
Description: The service boundary is the thing that keeps Juralio's Apache-2.0 licensing separate from this service's AGPL. Under AGPL section 5(c) a combination cannot be undone, so the boundary is worth defending automatically rather than by memory.
Acceptance Criteria: A build fails if either repository imports code from the other.

Summary: Add a CI check that fails on cross-repo imports
Description: Fail the build on any import, submodule, package dependency or shared build step spanning the two repositories. Also flag copied files by content hash against the service repo's tree.
Acceptance Criteria: A deliberately added cross-repo import fails CI with a message explaining why.

Summary: Licence compliance
Description: The combined deployment is AGPL-3.0. Apache-2.0 absorbs cleanly because every additional term it carries falls inside AGPL section 7's permitted list. Obligations are satisfied by a footer, a link and a release step - but they must exist before the first external user, not after. Drop this entire epic if a commercial licence is obtained.
Acceptance Criteria: Corresponding Source is offered to users from a network server, matching the deployed commit; all notices present.

Summary: Build the Corresponding Source publication pipeline
Description: AGPL section 13 requires a prominent offer of the Corresponding Source of the version users are actually interacting with. That means it belongs in the release pipeline, not in a manual process someone remembers.
Acceptance Criteria: Every production release automatically publishes matching source; the two cannot drift.

Summary: Create the public mirror repository and workflow
Description: A public repository holding the Corresponding Source. On a release tag, push the exact deployed tree to it. Secrets live in environment configuration rather than the repo, so nothing needs redacting - but verify that before the first push.
Acceptance Criteria: A release tag results in the matching commit appearing publicly; a gitleaks scan of the mirror is clean.

Summary: Gate deploys on a successful mirror push
Description: Ordering is tag, then mirror push, then deploy. If the mirror push fails the deploy does not proceed, so a running version always has published source behind it.
Acceptance Criteria: A simulated mirror failure blocks the deploy.

Summary: Serve the source offer from the application UI
Description: The offer must be prominent, from a network server, at no charge. A footer link resolving to the mirror at the running commit satisfies it. Wire the commit SHA into the build so the link is version-accurate.
Acceptance Criteria: The running application links to the exact source of the version being served.

Summary: Notices and attributions
Description: Both licences impose notice obligations that survive into the combined work. Neither is heavy; both are checkable.
Acceptance Criteria: Every notice obligation in the launch checklist is satisfied and verified.

Summary: Add AGPL modification and licence notices
Description: Section 5(a): a prominent notice that you modified the work, with a relevant date. Section 5(b): a prominent notice that it is released under AGPL. Section 5(d): Appropriate Legal Notices in the interactive UI - copyright notice, no-warranty statement, that recipients may convey the work, and how to view the licence. The root LICENSE is never deleted or altered; section 8 terminates your rights if it is.
Acceptance Criteria: All four notices present and reachable from the running application; LICENSE unmodified at the repo root.

Summary: Satisfy the Apache-2.0 notice obligations
Description: Section 4(a): ship a copy of the Apache License for the Juralio-derived portion. Section 4(b): retain existing copyright, patent, trademark and attribution notices, and mark files you changed. Section 4(c): reproduce any upstream NOTICE file attributions. Apache-licensed files keep their headers - it is the combination that is AGPL.
Acceptance Criteria: Apache licence and NOTICE attributions ship with the product; no Apache header has been stripped.

Summary: Run a trademark sweep
Description: AGPL section 7(e) and Apache section 6 both reserve trademark rights - neither licence grants you the upstream marks. Confirm no upstream name, logo, wordmark or domain survives in any user-visible surface, including email templates, error pages and the Word add-in manifest.
Acceptance Criteria: A full sweep finds no upstream trademark in any shipped surface.

Summary: Observability
Description: Establish what the service is doing in production. Logging must use the existing redaction helpers - this is privileged legal material, and a log line is a disclosure.
Acceptance Criteria: Structured logs, metrics, dashboards and alerts are live; no sensitive content reaches a log.

Summary: Structured logging and error reporting
Description: The codebase already separates user-facing errors from internal ones: httpError.ts keeps exception messages away from clients, and safeError.ts provides redaction helpers for logging. Build on those rather than adding a parallel path.
Acceptance Criteria: Every request is traceable; no document content or credential appears in any log.

Summary: Add structured request logging with redaction
Description: Request id, user id, route, status, duration. Route every log through the safeError redaction helpers. Verify explicitly that document content, prompts and API keys never appear.
Acceptance Criteria: Logs are queryable by request id and user id; a deliberate probe confirms no sensitive field is emitted.

Summary: Wire error tracking to the redaction helpers
Description: An error tracker that captures raw exception payloads would defeat the existing protections. Integrate through safeError so the redaction applies before anything leaves the process.
Acceptance Criteria: Errors reach the tracker with stack traces intact and sensitive values removed.

Summary: Metrics, dashboards and alerts
Description: The paths that fail quietly are the queue workers, the model provider calls and the conversion pipeline - all asynchronous, none visible to a user until something is missing.
Acceptance Criteria: A dashboard shows service health at a glance; alerts fire on the silent failure paths.

Summary: Instrument service and queue metrics
Description: Request rate, latency and error rate per route; queue depth, job duration and failure rate for conversion, extraction and export jobs; model provider latency, error and token consumption.
Acceptance Criteria: Metrics are collected and charted for all three areas.

Summary: Alert on the silent failure paths
Description: Queue backlog growth, repeated job failures, model provider errors, storage failures and migration failures. Each alert names the runbook that resolves it.
Acceptance Criteria: Each alert has fired at least once in a drill and resolved to a runbook.

Summary: Backend test safety net
Description: Coverage is gated at 52 percent statements on backend/src/lib, and the largest, most complex files sit inside that gap. The convention in the repo is a ratchet - floors only go up - so raise them as tests land.
Acceptance Criteria: The largest untested surfaces have characterisation tests and the coverage floors have been raised.

Summary: Cover the largest untested surfaces
Description: Prioritise by size and blast radius rather than chasing a percentage: tabular.ts at 2,650 lines, user.ts at 2,192, documentOps.ts at 2,013 and toolDispatcher.ts at 1,998.
Acceptance Criteria: Each named file has route or unit tests covering its main paths; the ratchet floors are raised in the same change.

Summary: Route integration tests for tabular.ts and user.ts
Description: The two largest route files. Cover the main success paths, the authorisation boundaries and the error handling, following the existing integration test patterns.
Acceptance Criteria: Both files have route integration coverage; a deliberate regression in each is caught.

Summary: Characterisation tests for the chat tool layer
Description: toolDispatcher.ts routes thirteen assistant tools and documentOps.ts implements the document operations. Characterise current behaviour before changing anything in this area.
Acceptance Criteria: Tool dispatch and document operations have tests describing actual current behaviour.

Summary: Raise the coverage ratchet floors
Description: Update the thresholds in backend/vitest.config.mts to the newly measured values, rounded down, in the same change as the tests. The repo convention is explicit that floors only move up.
Acceptance Criteria: New floors committed and CI fails on a drop below them.

Summary: Operational readiness
Description: Everything required to run this as a service holding confidential legal material, rather than as an application that happens to be deployed.
Acceptance Criteria: Backups restore, runbooks exist, and the service has been load tested.

Summary: Backup, restore and disaster recovery
Description: An untested backup is not a backup. For legal client data the restore path is the thing that matters, and it is worth proving before you need it.
Acceptance Criteria: A full restore has been performed into a clean environment and verified.

Summary: Configure automated backups and prove a restore
Description: Database and object storage both. Perform an actual restore into a clean environment and confirm documents, chats and reviews all come back intact and readable.
Acceptance Criteria: A restore drill completes with the application fully functional against the restored data.

Summary: Write runbooks for the common failure modes
Description: Queue backlog, model provider outage, storage failure, failed migration, certificate expiry, and the restore procedure. Each alert from the observability epic points at one of these.
Acceptance Criteria: Every alert resolves to a runbook a person can follow without prior context.

Summary: Performance and resilience
Description: The repository ships a k6 SSE load scenario because streaming is where this class of application falls over first.
Acceptance Criteria: Load testing is complete and what it surfaced has been addressed.

Summary: Run the k6 SSE load scenario against staging
Description: loadtest.yml already defines the scenario. Run it against real infrastructure rather than a laptop, with concurrent streaming chats plus tabular generation.
Acceptance Criteria: A load report exists with latency and error rate at the target concurrency.

Summary: Address what the load test surfaces
Description: Likely candidates from the review: connection handling under concurrent SSE, queue throughput when conversion and extraction compete, and provider rate limits.
Acceptance Criteria: Identified bottlenecks are fixed or explicitly accepted with a documented limit.

Summary: Launch
Description: Final verification and cutover. Nothing here should surface a surprise - if it does, the preceding sprints were not finished.
Acceptance Criteria: Production is live, verified, monitored, and licence-compliant.

Summary: Pre-launch verification
Description: One pass over everything, against production configuration rather than staging assumptions.
Acceptance Criteria: All suites green, compliance checklist signed off, security review complete.

Summary: Run the full suite against production configuration
Description: Backend, frontend, stack tests, schema drift and the Playwright e2e suite, against the production build and configuration.
Acceptance Criteria: Every suite green against production configuration.

Summary: Sign off the licence compliance checklist
Description: Ten items: LICENSE retained; modification notice with date; AGPL notice; Appropriate Legal Notices in the UI; prominent source offer matching the deployed commit; Apache licence copy; Apache notices retained and changed files marked; NOTICE attributions reproduced; no upstream trademarks; release ordering verified.
Acceptance Criteria: Every item checked against the running production application, not against intent.

Summary: Security review of the combined deployment
Description: The repository ships a security-review workflow. Run it across both repositories plus the integration seam, and treat the boundary itself as in scope.
Acceptance Criteria: Review complete; findings triaged and either fixed or accepted in writing.

Summary: Go live
Description: Cutover and the watched period immediately after it.
Acceptance Criteria: Production serving real users with monitoring confirmed working.

Summary: Production cutover and smoke test
Description: Deploy to production, run the smoke path end to end - signup, upload, chat with a document, run a workflow, run a tabular review, export - and confirm the source offer link resolves to the deployed commit.
Acceptance Criteria: Every smoke path passes against production; the source link resolves correctly.

Summary: Post-launch monitoring window
Description: A defined watch period with alerting confirmed live, a rollback rehearsed, and someone accountable for responding.
Acceptance Criteria: The window completes with no unresolved incident and alerting proven working.
